title: National Commission for Homoeopathy Clarifies Regulatory Position on Cross-Practice by Homoeopathic Practitioners
body_text:
The National Commission for Homoeopathy (NCH) has clarified its regulatory position regarding the practice of other systems of medicine by Homoeopathic practitioners, with a view to ensuring that the applicable provisions are understood and reported accurately and in their proper regulatory context.
As per Regulation 36(y) of the National Commission for Homoeopathy (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Code of Ethics for Practitioners of Homoeopathy) Regulations, 2022, a Homoeopathic practitioner shall not practise any other system of medicine other than Homoeopathy.
However, the proviso to Regulation 36(y) specifically provides that this restriction does not prevent or restrict a Homoeopathic medical practitioner from practising under a National Health Programme or any other programme run by the Central or State Government, provided that the practitioner has undergone the training or course recognised or prescribed by the competent authority.
The Commission has also drawn attention to Sub-regulation (7) of Regulation 14 of the National Commission for Homoeopathy (Homoeopathy Graduate Degree Course – Bachelor of Homoeopathic Medicine and Surgery (B.H.M.S.)) Regulations, 2022, which recognises the role of Homoeopathic medical graduates in Government health facilities and National Health Programmes.
The NCH has issued the clarification to ensure that the provisions of Regulation 36(y), including its proviso, are understood and reported accurately and in their proper regulatory context.

enrichment.summary: The National Commission for Homoeopathy (NCH) has issued a clarification on Regulation 36(y) of its 2022 Professional Conduct Regulations, which bars Homoeopathic practitioners from practising other systems of medicine. It clarifies that the regulation's proviso allows such practitioners to work under National Health Programmes or other Central/State government programmes, provided they have undergone the prescribed training. The NCH also cited Regulation 14(7) of the 2022 B.H.M.S. degree course regulations, which recognises the role of Homoeopathy graduates in government health facilities and national health programmes.
enrichment.context:
This clarification appears to be a response to media or public confusion/reports suggesting either a blanket ban or a blanket permission for Homoeopathic doctors to practise allopathy or other systems. The NCH, established under the National Commission for Homoeopathy Act, 2020 (replacing the earlier Central Council of Homoeopathy), regulates education and practice standards for Homoeopathy in India, similar to the National Medical Commission for allopathic medicine and the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine for AYUSH systems like Ayurveda, Unani, and Siddha.

The broader context relates to recurring debates in India over cross-pathy practice — i.e., whether AYUSH practitioners can prescribe allopathic medicines, especially in rural and underserved areas facing doctor shortages. Various states (e.g., Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra) have permitted limited allopathic practice by AYUSH doctors after bridge courses, sparking objections from bodies like the Indian Medical Association. This NCH clarification is narrower in scope, addressing only participation in government-run National Health Programmes (such as immunisation, TB control, or public health campaigns) after due training, not a general license for cross-system practice.
